BREAKING: CZ (founder of Binance) says it looks like Binance got hacked. more than $2.5 billion left its hot wallets, and Tether and Circle froze $1.8 billion of it within hours

hacks this size rarely start with code. the $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year started on one developer's laptop. one machine, one process nobody noticed

so last night I had Claude Code check mine. it found 18,742 webcam photos and video clips on my MacBook that I never knowingly recorded. the oldest folder was 14 months old. the newest was from that morning

I opened the previews expecting forgotten video calls. instead I saw my desk after midnight, friends walking through the room and an empty chair while a conversation continued in the kitchen

the files were buried in an application's storage folder. each had a timestamp, and the videos had audio. none appeared in Photos or the folder where I normally saved recordings

I made a backup and had Claude inspect the copy. it grouped the files by date, checked their metadata and traced the directory to a background capture app configured to launch when I logged in

then I checked the original folder. the latest clip had been created 12 seconds earlier. it showed me leaning toward the screen, opening the same files I was now reviewing

Claude checked the running processes and identified the recorder. I stopped it and watched the folder for another 10 minutes. no new files appeared. the final clip ended with me reaching for the keyboard to shut it down

You can't stop the next exchange hack. you can make sure it doesn't start on your laptop. the prompt that found the recorder on mine is in the first reply

the model is the engine. the harness is the job. i gave the night shift to my AI employee

"do not merge or change anything on your own" was the line i cared about most. it's the one he takes most literally.

he reads, compares, diagnoses and drafts. i decide. the three PRs sat there with "Waiting for approval" until i opened them.

that's how Viktor is built: every action that matters waits for a human yes. he can prepare everything. he can't push it through.every night at 2:00, someone runs all 412 evals on my agent harness, reads every failed run and compares it with the night before.
it isn't me anymore
meet Viktor ↓
 
i spent months building the harness around my agent. the context, the tools, the loop, the evals, the rules. that part i like.
the part i never liked comes after: running the suite every single day, opening every red run, and figuring out whether yesterday's prompt edit broke something or a test just timed out again.
that isn't building. that's a shift. so i hired someone for it.
his name is Viktor. he lives in our Slack, connects to 9,800+ tools and already works on 70,000+ teams. on mine he has one job: the nightly evals.
i built the harness. he runs it every night. i still make every call.

→ Usability: can it read pricing and fill your forms
→ Payments: can it actually check out

→ pricing that stays empty until JavaScript loads
→ buttons and fields with no labels
→ popups that cover the whole page

8. Show me a before and after checklist of every fix.

The stores agents can use will win.

The ones that block them are betting the agents come back.

They won't.

virals.text:
Someone turned the hardest parts of LLM inference engineering into a course where you have to fix the performance problems yourself.

And you can do it on a Mac.

The project is called tiny-llm, an open-source course for building a miniature vLLM-style inference engine around Qwen3.

It starts with a simple implementation using matrix operations. You build attention, normalization, positional encoding, the Transformer layers, and the loop that generates tokens.

You have a working model.

Now the interesting engineering begins.

During decoding, repeatedly processing the previous tokens wastes computation. So you implement a KV cache and reuse previously computed attention state.

Next, you look at model weights. Keeping everything in dense BF16 consumes memory bandwidth. So you retain packed 4-bit weights and implement specialized matrix operations.

Then you move into Metal kernels, SIMD matrix operations, fused RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, and tiled prefill attention.

Once the single-request engine works, you tackle a different problem.

What happens when multiple requests arrive, each with different prompt lengths and different amounts of cached state?

You implement continuous batching, chunked prefill, paged KV storage, and attention that reads directly from noncontiguous cache pages.

The four-week curriculum eventually extends into a small coding-agent harness with validated tool calls, checkpoints, context management, and evaluation.

Every stage comes with exercises, reference implementations, tests, and measurements to help you understand the behavior of the system you're building.

The course uses MLX, C++, and Metal on Apple Silicon. You don't need an NVIDIA GPU, and the introductory path supports Qwen3-0.6B on an 8GB Mac.

Some later checkpoints remain under development and review, but there's already a substantial amount of real inference engineering to learn from.

The GitHub repo has crossed 4,800 stars.

Someone built a web browser that doesn't render webpages.

It has passed 37K GitHub stars as a project written in Zig from scratch, rather than forked from Chromium.

And in the team's benchmark, it used 16× less memory than headless Chrome.

It's called Lightpanda, a browser designed specifically for AI agents, web scraping, and automation.

Here's what makes the architecture interesting.

A traditional browser has to fetch resources, parse HTML, execute JavaScript, maintain the DOM, calculate layouts, and render graphics.

But an AI agent often needs only a subset of that functionality. It needs to navigate pages, inspect elements, execute scripts, click buttons, fill forms, and extract data.

Lightpanda implements the browser machinery needed for those tasks without a graphical rendering engine.

Under the hood:
→ Zig for the core browser implementation
→ V8 for JavaScript execution
→ html5ever for HTML parsing
→ DOM and Web APIs for interacting with pages
→ CDP and WebDriver BiDi for browser automation
→ Native MCP tools for AI agent integration

It can work with existing automation clients, including Playwright, Puppeteer, and Selenium, subject to its supported browser APIs.

In its published 100-page benchmark, Lightpanda completed the workload in roughly 5 seconds using 123 MB peak memory. Headless Chrome took 46 seconds and peaked at 2 GB.

Those numbers are workload-specific, but the architectural idea is compelling.

The project has now reached version 1.0 and passes more than 1.7 million Web Platform Tests subtests. Compatibility still isn't equivalent to Chrome, especially for visual rendering and layout.

For automated systems that mostly need to interact with the DOM, this is a fascinating alternative to running a full graphical browser engine.

Fully open source.

AI developers are wasting thousands of dollars rebuilding tools that already exist.

you get an idea for an agent, spend an entire weekend building its memory, browser, and workflow from scratch, only to discover open-source projects that already do it better.

there's a GitHub repo mapping 300+ AI agent projects across 36 categories.

here are a few worth exploring:

→ DSPy: optimize prompts programmatically

→ Serena: smarter code understanding and editing

→ Stagehand: automate real websites with AI

→ Steel Browser: isolated browser environments for agents

→ Cognee: persistent AI memory

→ Screenpipe: give agents context about your computer activity

→ Google ADK: build and evaluate agent workflows

→ Opik: trace and debug agent runs

my rule: find the category, compare three tools, check which are actively maintained, then build.

don't waste weeks reinventing something the open-source community already solved.

the repo also includes JSON and YAML exports for your own tools.

free to access. MIT licensed. no signup.

virals.text:
Claude Code signs every commit it makes for you with "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5", and ends every PR description with "🤖 Generated with Claude Code". One line in your settings 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝘁 𝗼𝗳𝗳.

In ~/.claude/settings.json, add this inside the outermost { }:
"attribution": false

This needs Claude Code 2.1.281 or later. Older versions don't recognize it and 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲, so the permissions and hooks you set up in it stop working too. Run claude --version first. If it's older, run claude update.

To turn it off in just one project, put it in that project's .claude/settings.local.json instead. That only applies to you.

The old "includeCoAuthoredBy": false is deprecated. If you have it, swap it for attribution.

virals.name: Daily Dose of Data Science
virals.text:
Layers of observability in AI systems, explained visually:

If an LLM app is serving real users, its input and output are not enough to debug it.

Consider a RAG pipeline where a query passes through embedding, retrieval, context assembly, and generation.

Every operation adds latency, may call a paid API, and can fail while still producing a valid-looking response.

Traces and spans provide visibility.

- A trace records the full path of one request. The Trace column runs from query to response.

- A span records one operation within that trace. The colored boxes are spans.

Each span captures:

> Query span

The input, timestamp, session identifier, and request metadata.

> Embedding span

The model, input size, latency, retries, and rate-limit errors.

> Retrieval span

The retrieved chunks, document IDs, relevance scores, filters, top-k value, and latency. Many RAG failures originate here. Without these fields, there is no evidence that retrieval selected the wrong documents.

> Context span

The context assembled from retrieved chunks, instructions, and conversation history. This catches truncated documents, duplicated chunks, missing citations, and prompts exceeding the token budget.

> Generation span

The model, token counts, time to first token, total latency, finish reason, retries, and estimated cost.

With these details, a bad response can now be traced to retrieval, context assembly, or generation.

To use this in practice, Opik already implements this observability infrastructure for LLM apps and is open source.

It captures traces and spans across LLM calls, retrieval steps, and tool executions, with latency, token usage, and cost attached to each operation.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/Nc3NQzo8Hl

(don't forget to star it ⭐)

In Opik, every operation belonging to one request carries the same Trace ID. If the app processes 1,000 requests, it creates 1,000 traces, each containing its own spans.

This makes cost analysis more useful. Instead of aggregate spend, teams can identify the model calls, retries, or oversized prompts responsible.

Over time, changes in retrieval scores, embedding latency, or context size become visible before they turn into broader quality problems.

That said, observability is one of eight areas we would learn for building production LLM systems.

We covered all eight in the 2026 LLM Engineering Roadmap, with free and open-source resources for each one.

Read it below.

New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

outsiders.name: Tech with Mak
outsiders.text:
Someone turned the hardest parts of LLM inference engineering into a course where you have to fix the performance problems yourself.

And you can do it on a Mac.

The project is called tiny-llm, an open-source course for building a miniature vLLM-style inference engine around Qwen3.

It starts with a simple implementation using matrix operations. You build attention, normalization, positional encoding, the Transformer layers, and the loop that generates tokens.

You have a working model.

Now the interesting engineering begins.

During decoding, repeatedly processing the previous tokens wastes computation. So you implement a KV cache and reuse previously computed attention state.

Next, you look at model weights. Keeping everything in dense BF16 consumes memory bandwidth. So you retain packed 4-bit weights and implement specialized matrix operations.

Then you move into Metal kernels, SIMD matrix operations, fused RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, and tiled prefill attention.

Once the single-request engine works, you tackle a different problem.

What happens when multiple requests arrive, each with different prompt lengths and different amounts of cached state?

You implement continuous batching, chunked prefill, paged KV storage, and attention that reads directly from noncontiguous cache pages.

The four-week curriculum eventually extends into a small coding-agent harness with validated tool calls, checkpoints, context management, and evaluation.

Every stage comes with exercises, reference implementations, tests, and measurements to help you understand the behavior of the system you're building.

The course uses MLX, C++, and Metal on Apple Silicon. You don't need an NVIDIA GPU, and the introductory path supports Qwen3-0.6B on an 8GB Mac.

Some later checkpoints remain under development and review, but there's already a substantial amount of real inference engineering to learn from.

The GitHub repo has crossed 4,800 stars.

Someone built a web browser that doesn't render webpages.

It has passed 37K GitHub stars as a project written in Zig from scratch, rather than forked from Chromium.

And in the team's benchmark, it used 16× less memory than headless Chrome.

It's called Lightpanda, a browser designed specifically for AI agents, web scraping, and automation.

Here's what makes the architecture interesting.

A traditional browser has to fetch resources, parse HTML, execute JavaScript, maintain the DOM, calculate layouts, and render graphics.

But an AI agent often needs only a subset of that functionality. It needs to navigate pages, inspect elements, execute scripts, click buttons, fill forms, and extract data.

Lightpanda implements the browser machinery needed for those tasks without a graphical rendering engine.

Under the hood:
→ Zig for the core browser implementation
→ V8 for JavaScript execution
→ html5ever for HTML parsing
→ DOM and Web APIs for interacting with pages
→ CDP and WebDriver BiDi for browser automation
→ Native MCP tools for AI agent integration

It can work with existing automation clients, including Playwright, Puppeteer, and Selenium, subject to its supported browser APIs.

In its published 100-page benchmark, Lightpanda completed the workload in roughly 5 seconds using 123 MB peak memory. Headless Chrome took 46 seconds and peaked at 2 GB.

Those numbers are workload-specific, but the architectural idea is compelling.

The project has now reached version 1.0 and passes more than 1.7 million Web Platform Tests subtests. Compatibility still isn't equivalent to Chrome, especially for visual rendering and layout.

For automated systems that mostly need to interact with the DOM, this is a fascinating alternative to running a full graphical browser engine.

Fully open source.

AI developers are wasting thousands of dollars rebuilding tools that already exist.

you get an idea for an agent, spend an entire weekend building its memory, browser, and workflow from scratch, only to discover open-source projects that already do it better.

there's a GitHub repo mapping 300+ AI agent projects across 36 categories.

here are a few worth exploring:

→ DSPy: optimize prompts programmatically

→ Serena: smarter code understanding and editing

→ Stagehand: automate real websites with AI

→ Steel Browser: isolated browser environments for agents

→ Cognee: persistent AI memory

→ Screenpipe: give agents context about your computer activity

→ Google ADK: build and evaluate agent workflows

→ Opik: trace and debug agent runs

my rule: find the category, compare three tools, check which are actively maintained, then build.

don't waste weeks reinventing something the open-source community already solved.

the repo also includes JSON and YAML exports for your own tools.

free to access. MIT licensed. no signup.

outsiders.name: Daily Dose of Data Science
outsiders.text:
Layers of observability in AI systems, explained visually:

If an LLM app is serving real users, its input and output are not enough to debug it.

Consider a RAG pipeline where a query passes through embedding, retrieval, context assembly, and generation.

Every operation adds latency, may call a paid API, and can fail while still producing a valid-looking response.

Traces and spans provide visibility.

- A trace records the full path of one request. The Trace column runs from query to response.

- A span records one operation within that trace. The colored boxes are spans.

Each span captures:

> Query span

The input, timestamp, session identifier, and request metadata.

> Embedding span

The model, input size, latency, retries, and rate-limit errors.

> Retrieval span

The retrieved chunks, document IDs, relevance scores, filters, top-k value, and latency. Many RAG failures originate here. Without these fields, there is no evidence that retrieval selected the wrong documents.

> Context span

The context assembled from retrieved chunks, instructions, and conversation history. This catches truncated documents, duplicated chunks, missing citations, and prompts exceeding the token budget.

> Generation span

The model, token counts, time to first token, total latency, finish reason, retries, and estimated cost.

With these details, a bad response can now be traced to retrieval, context assembly, or generation.

To use this in practice, Opik already implements this observability infrastructure for LLM apps and is open source.

It captures traces and spans across LLM calls, retrieval steps, and tool executions, with latency, token usage, and cost attached to each operation.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/Nc3NQzo8Hl

(don't forget to star it ⭐)

In Opik, every operation belonging to one request carries the same Trace ID. If the app processes 1,000 requests, it creates 1,000 traces, each containing its own spans.

This makes cost analysis more useful. Instead of aggregate spend, teams can identify the model calls, retries, or oversized prompts responsible.

Over time, changes in retrieval scores, embedding latency, or context size become visible before they turn into broader quality problems.

That said, observability is one of eight areas we would learn for building production LLM systems.

We covered all eight in the 2026 LLM Engineering Roadmap, with free and open-source resources for each one.

Read it below.
